title: Interpreting results
summary: O, Ω, and Θ as bound language; comparing algorithms and relative growth. The CPU vs GPU panel connects theory with practice without confusing asymptotic order with raw chip speed.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish upper, lower, and tight bounds and relate them to available numeric and symbolic evidence.
Explain why asymptotic order does not depend on hardware and how execution in different environments still illustrates practical effects.

terms.label: dominant term
terms.definition: In a polynomial or sum of terms in n, the fastest-growing term that determines asymptotic order when lower-order terms and constants are ignored.

content.text: O upper-bounds, Ω lower-bounds, and Θ means both match in order. In practice multiplicative constants and lower-order terms are dropped: the
sets the order (e.g. n² + 1000n behaves like n² for large n).

blocks.latex: 1 < \log n < n < n\log n < n^2 < n^3 < 2^n < n!

content.text: Comparing algorithms often uses limits of cost-function ratios: 0, ∞, or a constant tells you which grows faster or whether they share order. The tool may show comparisons to support decisions when the contract allows.
Asymptotic complexity describes how work scales with n, not milliseconds on a specific CPU. Therefore
hardware does not change the growth order
you study in class. Still, observing execution across environments (e.g. CPU vs GPU) helps relate growth differences to practice when parallelism or memory bottlenecks matter.

blocks.title: How to read the panel without contradicting theory

content.text: Treat the panel as guidance on structural suitability (parallelism, access patterns), not as a scientific benchmark. Do not invent timings or claim asymptotic improvements just because the panel suggests an environment: formal analysis still rules the order.
Do not use the GPU/CPU panel to “prove” an O(·) bound: use it to connect practical intuition with the theoretical model you already justified with counting and structure.
